name: Auth

hero.title: Sign-in where the unsafe options don't exist.
hero.lede: One `useOidc` call signs users in with Google, Keycloak, Auth0, Entra or any OpenID Connect provider, on the web and, from the same source, on iOS and Android. Sessions, passkeys, TOTP, attempt limiting and an open-redirect-proof guard come with it, all on Web Crypto and `fetch`.

why.title: The code you least want to write yourself.

items.title: Secure defaults you can't turn down
items.text: Authorization code with S256 PKCE, `state` and `nonce`, the RFC 9207 issuer check, https-only endpoints, single-use flows that expire in ten minutes. The implicit flow, the password grant and PKCE `plain` are not offered at all.

items.title: No callback handler to write
items.text: On the redirect page `useOidc` scrubs the code from the address bar and history, checks `state` in constant time, exchanges the code and verifies the ID token. `status()` reads `signedIn` only after the signature and nonce check out.

items.title: One call, three platforms
items.text: The same `useOidc` compiles to `ASWebAuthenticationSession` on iOS and a Custom Tab on Android, with the session in the Keychain or Keystore. `status()` strings and `error()` codes are identical on all three, and a shared set of signed test tokens must get the same verdict from the web, Swift and Kotlin verifiers.

items.title: The rest of a login, server side
items.text: HMAC-signed `__Host-` session cookies with secret rotation and revocation, RFC 6238 TOTP with replay protection, WebAuthn passkeys (ES256, and RS256 for Windows Hello), and a bounded attempt limiter.

before.label: Auth.js (next-auth 4) in Next.js
before.caption: A server route holding a client secret, a session provider around the app, and a hook with a loading state.

after.label: with @pyreon/auth
after.caption: A public client with PKCE: no server route, no secret in your app. The redirect page completes the sign-in by itself.

demo.title: Sign in, then try to break it.
demo.text: This runs the real `useOidc` against an OpenID provider living inside the page. Sign in normally, then switch the provider into a misbehaving mode and sign in again: a replayed token, a forged signature, an issuer mix-up. Each one is stopped by a named check.
demo.referenceHtml:
Acmesigned out
what the package does
demo.spec: DemoAuth mounts the real `useOidc` with the in-page provider from `docs/src/examples/auth/fake-provider.ts` (real discovery, S256 PKCE and ES256-signed ID tokens; only the network and the login page are simulated). The step list animates as before, except the last step reads "claims verified; status() is signedIn" (useOidc does not schedule refreshes by itself on the web). A mode switch sets the provider's `mode`: honest → signedIn; wrong-nonce → error `bad_nonce`; forged-key → `bad_signature`; mix-up → `issuer_mismatch`; deny → `provider_error`. The failing step turns red and shows the code from `auth.error()`.

items.name: `createAuth`
items.text: the same state machine with every dependency explicit, for servers and backends-for-frontends with a shared `FlowStore`.

items.name: Refresh that can't switch users
items.text: a refreshed ID token must name the same `sub`, or the session is cleared with `subject_changed`.

items.name: Key rotation without restarts
items.text: `createJwksCache` refetches the provider's keys once when a token names an unknown `kid`.

items.name: Provider presets
items.text: `google`, `keycloak(base, realm)`, and OAuth2 metadata for `github`, `facebook()` or any `oauth2(…)` provider.

items.name: Signed sessions
items.text: `signSession` / `verifySession` / `sessionCookie`: HMAC-SHA-256, secrets of 32+ characters, `isRevoked` for logout-everywhere.

items.name: TOTP
items.text: `generateTotpSecret`, `totp`, `verifyTotp` with ±1 step and a `lastUsedStep` so a code works once.

items.name: Passkeys
items.text: `verifyRegistration` and `verifyAssertion`; user verification on by default, a non-increasing `signCount` rejected.

items.name: `createAttemptLimiter`
items.text: per-key windows, bounded memory, and a flood of new keys can't buy a blocked key a fresh budget.

items.name: `createGuard` + `safeReturnTo`
items.text: route guards whose `returnTo` is checked with the browser's own URL parser, so `//evil.example` and tab tricks go home.

api.title: Everything the docs cover, from one import.

limits.title: A web reload starts signed out, on purpose
limits.text: Browser tokens live in memory, never in `localStorage`, so one XSS bug can't steal a long-lived session. To stay signed in, call `signIn()` on load (the provider usually answers without a prompt) or keep the session on your server with `signSession`.

limits.title: Several servers need a shared flow store
limits.text: Pending sign-ins live in one process by default. Implement `FlowStore` over Redis or similar, with an atomic `take`.

limits.title: GitHub and Facebook are OAuth2, not OIDC
limits.text: There is no verified identity to read, so use `createAuth` with their `metadata` and fetch the user from their API.

limits.title: Android needs two manifest entries
limits.text: Declare `PyreonAuthActivity` and `PyreonAuthRedirectActivity` with your redirect scheme. iOS needs no setup for sign-in.

related.name: Query
related.text: Put the user in the `queryKey` and the bearer header in `queryFn`; it works on iOS and Android too.

related.name: HTTP
related.text: `bearer()` and `refresh()` middleware attach and renew the token on the web.

end.title: Sign-in, minus the afternoon of reading RFCs. We read them.

comingFrom.title: From a server route and a session provider to one call.
comingFrom.note: Different shapes: Auth.js keeps the session on your server with a client secret; `useOidc` is a public client with PKCE. Want a server session too? `createAuth` with a shared `FlowStore` plus `signSession` is the backend-for-frontend version.

comingFrom.title: Keep the components, bring your own provider.
comingFrom.note: Clerk is a hosted user service with its own sign-in UI. `@pyreon/auth` is a library: you choose the identity provider (Keycloak, Auth0, Zitadel, Entra, Google) and own the screens.

recipes.title: A second factor, then a session cookie
recipes.text: Throttle the guess, check the authenticator code once, and hand the browser a signed `__Host-` cookie instead of tokens.

recipes.title: An admin route that can't be bounced off-site
recipes.text: `createGuard` returns `true` or a login redirect carrying a safe `returnTo`.

recipes.title: Call your API from web, iOS and Android
recipes.text: The bearer header is built inside `queryFn`, and the user is part of the key, so signing in as someone else refetches.

faq.a: It is on `main` and ships with the next release; until then the npm `latest` does not include it. Everything on this page describes `main`.
No. It is a library. Your identity provider (Google, Keycloak, Auth0, Okta, Zitadel, Entra, anything that speaks OpenID Connect) holds the users; the package does the protocol and the checks.

faq.q: How do I know the checks work?
faq.a: The interop suite runs against `oidc-provider`, a certified OpenID Provider, in-process. The web, Swift and Kotlin verifiers judge one shared file of signed test tokens and must agree down to the error code. The demo above shows three attacks being refused, each by a named check.
On the web, in memory only. On iOS and Android, in the Keychain or Keystore, so the app stays signed in after a relaunch and refreshes an expired session on launch.
No password storage or hashing. It covers the sign-in protocol, sessions, second factors and passkeys; password sign-in belongs to your identity provider.
